claim: The N2pc is an event-related potential component that reliably indexes selective attention in humans and monkeys.
source: For instance, event-related potential (ERP) components like the N2pc (Eimer, 1996; Luck and Hillyard, 1994; Woodman and Luck, 1999) and Pd (Hickey et al., 2009) reliably index selective attention in humans and monkeys, alike.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The Pd is an event-related potential component that reliably indexes selective attention in humans and monkeys.
source: For instance, event-related potential (ERP) components like the N2pc (Eimer, 1996; Luck and Hillyard, 1994; Woodman and Luck, 1999) and Pd (Hickey et al., 2009) reliably index selective attention in humans and monkeys, alike.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The interpretation of extracortical measures of attention is severely limited by uncertainty about the exact neural processes that generate these signals.
source: However, the interpretation of these extracortical measures of attention is severely limited by uncertainty about the exact neural processes that generate these signals (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Understanding what brain processes an electric field indicates requires knowing how it is generated.
source: Understanding what brain processes an electric field indicates requires knowing how it is generated (e.g., Cohen, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Most EEG signals are hypothesized to be generated by interlaminar interactions in cortical columns.
source: For example, most EEG signals are hypothesized to be generated by interlaminar interactions in cortical columns (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Columnar microcircuits are ubiquitous across the brain.
source: Columnar microcircuits are ubiquitous across the brain (Douglas et al., 1989; Douglas and Martin, 1991), having a well-defined anatomical structure (Mountcastle, 1997; Kaas, 2012) and consistent physiological activation pattern (Bastos et al., 2012 but see Godlove et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Columnar microcircuits have a well-defined anatomical structure.
source: Columnar microcircuits are ubiquitous across the brain (Douglas et al., 1989; Douglas and Martin, 1991), having a well-defined anatomical structure (Mountcastle, 1997; Kaas, 2012) and consistent physiological activation pattern (Bastos et al., 2012 but see Godlove et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Columnar microcircuits have a consistent physiological activation pattern.
source: Columnar microcircuits are ubiquitous across the brain (Douglas et al., 1989; Douglas and Martin, 1991), having a well-defined anatomical structure (Mountcastle, 1997; Kaas, 2012) and consistent physiological activation pattern (Bastos et al., 2012 but see Godlove et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research, though one citation (Godlove et al., 2014) suggests potential exceptions.

claim: The relationship between functional architecture and electric fields related to cognition commonly measured in humans is unexplored.
source: The canonical cortical microcircuit offers a framework in which to interpret columnar dynamics in sensory or cognitive tasks, yet the relationship between this functional architecture and electric fields related to cognition commonly measured in humans is unexplored.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the state of the field.

claim: Electric fields measured at the surface of the brain (ECoG) and scalp (EEG) are theorized to be generated by dipoles in cortex.
source: Electric fields measured at the surface of the brain (ECoG) and scalp (EEG) are theorized to be generated by dipoles in cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about EEG/ECoG generation.

claim: Measuring current dipoles requires sampling electrical potentials across all the layers of the cerebral cortex.
source: However, measuring current dipoles requires sampling electrical potentials across all the layers of the cerebral cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about measuring current dipoles.

claim: Laminar neurophysiological measurements are rare and unsystematic in humans.
source: Such laminar neurophysiological measurements are rare and unsystematic in humans.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the state of the field.

claim: Work in rodents has uncovered insights into cortical laminar microcircuits underlying evoked EEG signals, but all were limited to sensory responses.
source: Work in rodents has uncovered intriguing insights into cortical laminar microcircuits underlying evoked EEG signals, but all of these were limited to sensory responses (Jellema et al., 2004; Bruyns-Haylett et al., 2017; Nass et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Macaque monkeys produce homologues of the attention-associated EEG signals N2pc and Pd.
source: Fortunately, macaque monkeys produce homologues of the attention-associated EEG signals (N2pc: Woodman et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2009; Purcell et al., 2013; Pd: Cosman et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Laminar neurophysiological measurements are well established in macaques.
source: Laminar neurophysiological measurements (Schroeder et al., 1998; Maier et al., 2010; Buffalo et al., 2011; Hansen et al., 2011; Self et al., 2013; Godlove et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2016; Hembrook-Short et al., 2017; Nandy et al., 2017; Trautmann et al., 2019; Westerberg et al., 2019; Tovar et al., 2020; Ferro et al., 2021) and EEG (Schmid et al., 2006; Woodman et al., 2007; Sandhaeger et al., 2019) are well established in macaques.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: EEG is well established in macaques.
source: Laminar neurophysiological measurements (Schroeder et al., 1998; Maier et al., 2010; Buffalo et al., 2011; Hansen et al., 2011; Self et al., 2013; Godlove et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2016; Hembrook-Short et al., 2017; Nandy et al., 2017; Trautmann et al., 2019; Westerberg et al., 2019; Tovar et al., 2020; Ferro et al., 2021) and EEG (Schmid et al., 2006; Woodman et al., 2007; Sandhaeger et al., 2019) are well established in macaques.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Little is known about the laminar origins of ERPs in primates.
source: However, despite many studies linking intra- and extracortical signals (Schroeder et al., 1992; Whittingstall and Logothetis, 2009; Musall et al., 2014; Snyder and Smith, 2015), to date, little is known about the laminar origins of ERPs in primates.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the state of the field, despite citing studies that have linked intra- and extracortical signals.

claim: Visual cortex generates dipoles through layer-specific transsynaptic currents that give rise to electric fields that track the deployment of selective attention.
source: Here, we show that visual cortex generates dipoles through layer-specific transsynaptic currents that give rise to electric fields that track the deployment of selective attention.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The dipoles were generated by the extragranular compartments of cortex.
source: These dipoles were generated by the extragranular compartments of cortex, indicating these cognitive operations likely arise from top-down interactions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The cognitive operations likely arise from top-down interactions.
source: These dipoles were generated by the extragranular compartments of cortex, indicating these cognitive operations likely arise from top-down interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that dipoles were generated by extragranular compartments, which are known to receive top-down inputs.

claim: Functional architecture was associated with the relative contribution of individual, local cortical columns to the global electric field.
source: Moreover, functional architecture – in the form of feature columns – was associated with the relative contribution of individual, local cortical columns to the global electric field.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: These results are the first to describe laminar specificity in synaptic activations contributing to the generation of electric fields associated with cognitive processing.
source: These results are the first to our knowledge to describe laminar specificity in synaptic activations contributing to the generation of electric fields associated with cognitive processing.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the novelty of their findings.

claim: Three macaque monkeys (Ca, He, and Z) performed visual search for an oddball color target presented within an array of five or seven uniform distractors.
source: Three macaque monkeys (designated Ca, He, and Z) performed visual search for an oddball color target (red or green), presented within an array of five or seven uniform distractors (green or red) (N sessions for each monkey: Ca 21, He 9, Z 18).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: A fourth monkey (P) performed visual search for an oddball shape presented within an array of up to seven uniform distractors.
source: A fourth monkey (P) performed visual search for an oddball shape (T or L) presented within an array of up to seven uniform distractors (L or T) (N sessions: monkey P, 22).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Each animal performed well above chance in the visual search task.
source: Each animal performed well above chance (chance level for monkeys Ca, He: 16.6%; P, Z: 12.5%) (behavioral accuracy in color search: Ca 88%, He 81%, Z 85%, shape search monkey P 66%).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral accuracy data reported.

claim: The N2pc was significant in monkey Z.
source: The N2pc was significant (dependent samples t test between polarizations averaged between 125 and 250 ms after array presentation (t(35) = 2.42, p = 0.02)).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the EEG data.

claim: Inverse solution of current distribution using sLORETA showed current density concentrated beneath electrode P6 caudal to the lunate sulcus and in area V4 on the prelunate gyrus.
source: Current density is concentrated beneath electrode P6 caudal to the lunate sulcus and in area V4 on the prelunate gyrus.
evidence: This is supported by the inverse modeling analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Previous source estimates for the N2pc identified the human homologue of V4.
source: Previous source estimates for the N2pc identified the human homologue of V4 (Luck and Hillyard, 1990; Luck and Hillyard, 1994; Hopf et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Areas in mid-level visual cortex in monkeys produce robust attention signals.
source: These findings are consistent with numerous reports that areas in mid-level visual cortex in monkeys produce robust attention signals (Moran and Desimone, 1985; Luck et al., 1997a; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Reynolds et al., 1999; Fries et al., 2001; see Roe et al., 2012 for review) across cortical layers (Engel et al., 2016; Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Attention signals are produced across cortical layers in mid-level visual cortex.
source: These findings are consistent with numerous reports that areas in mid-level visual cortex in monkeys produce robust attention signals (Moran and Desimone, 1985; Luck et al., 1997a; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Reynolds et al., 1999; Fries et al., 2001; see Roe et al., 2012 for review) across cortical layers (Engel et al., 2016; Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The inverse solution identifies V1 to be about as strong as V4 in contributing to the N2pc, which is unlikely given current knowledge on attentional modulation for each area.
source: Notably, the inverse solution identifies V1 to be about as strong as V4 in contributing to the N2pc, which is unlikely given current knowledge on attentional modulation for each area (Motter, 1993; Luck et al., 1997a; Kastner et al., 1999; Buffalo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on the inverse modeling results and comparison with cited literature on attentional modulation.

claim: Linear multielectrode arrays were inserted into area V4 of monkeys Ca and He perpendicular to the cortical surface, spanning supragranular, granular, and infragranular cortical layers.
source: Guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), linear multielectrode arrays (LMAs) were inserted into area V4 of monkeys Ca and He. LMAs were placed perpendicular to the cortical surface, spanning supragranular (L2/3), granular (L4), and infragranular (L5/6) cortical layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Attentional modulation of spiking activity could be observed during pop-out search performance consistent with previous reports.
source: We confirmed that attentional modulation of spiking activity could be observed during pop-out search performance consistent with previous reports (Westerberg et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: The laminar profile of attentional modulation matched that of attentional modulation in a different task with spiking activity in the middle layers being the most highly enhanced with attention.
source: Moreover, the laminar profile of attentional modulation matched that of attentional modulation in a different task with spiking activity in the middle layers being the most highly enhanced with attention (Figure 2; Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citation to previous work.

claim: Attentional modulation is present in the laminar data prior to the emergence of extracortical attention-associated fields such as the N2pc.
source: Critically, while attentional modulation is present in the laminar data prior to the emergence of extracortical attention-associated fields such as the N2pc, that cross-laminar modulation persists through this interval.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cross-laminar attentional modulation persists through the N2pc interval.
source: Critically, while attentional modulation is present in the laminar data prior to the emergence of extracortical attention-associated fields such as the N2pc, that cross-laminar modulation persists through this interval.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Significant differences in magnitude of attention effect across laminar compartment were detected for LFP.
source: Significant differences in magnitude of attention effect, averaged 150–190 ms after search array onset, across laminar compartment were detected through an ANOVA for both LFP (F(2, 442) = 22.43, p = 5.2e–10) and MUA (F(2, 442) = 3.87, p = 0.022).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the laminar data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Significant differences in magnitude of attention effect across laminar compartment were detected for MUA.
source: Significant differences in magnitude of attention effect, averaged 150–190 ms after search array onset, across laminar compartment were detected through an ANOVA for both LFP (F(2, 442) = 22.43, p = 5.2e–10) and MUA (F(2, 442) = 3.87, p = 0.022).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the laminar data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The effect of attention in the MUA was largest in the middle layers.
source: Note the effect of attention in the MUA was largest in the middle layers (ML2/3 = 2.68, ML4 = 3.50, ML5/6 = 2.38), consistent with previous reports (Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citation to previous work.

claim: Presentation of the search array in any configuration elicited an early current sink in L4, followed by a prolonged sink in L2/3 that was associated with a briefer source in L5/6.
source: Averaged across sessions, we observed that the electric field during the N2pc interval (Figure 4A) was associated with a consistent CSD pattern (Figure 4B). This relationship was observed in each monkey (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Presentation of the search array in any configuration elicited an early current sink in L4, followed by a prolonged sink in L2/3 that was associated with a briefer source in L5/6.
evidence: This is supported by the CSD data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All cortical layers provided significant information transmission in >75% of sessions during the N2pc window.
source: We next computed information transmission about target location from the CSD to the extracortical signal for each session (Figure 4C). All cortical layers provided significant information transmission in >75% of sessions during the N2pc window (150–190 ms following array onset).
evidence: This is supported by the information theoretic analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The magnitude of transmitted target information was significantly greater in L2/3 and L5/6 relative to L4.
source: However, the magnitude of transmitted target information was significantly greater in L2/3 and L5/6 relative to L4 (L2/3-L4: t(29) = 2.15, p = 0.040; L5/6-L4: t(29) = 2.20, p = 0.036).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the information transmission data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The magnitude of information transmission was not significantly different between L2/3 and L5/6.
source: The magnitude of information transmission was not significantly different between L2/3 and L5/6 (t(29) = 0.21, p = 0.84).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the information transmission data.

claim: Significant information transmission during the N2pc was observed in each monkey.
source: Moreover, significant information transmission during the N2pc was observed in each monkey (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the information theoretic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No signal differences or significant information transmission were found in the 100 ms pre-array baseline period.
source: Importantly, we found no signal differences or significant information transmission in the 100 ms pre-array baseline period as expected with baseline correction.
evidence: This is supported by the information theoretic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A polarization reversal in the extracortical signal was observed 200–250 ms following array presentation, likely corresponding to the Pd.
source: We also evaluated the interval 200–250 ms following array presentation and found a polarization reversal in the extracortical signal likely corresponding to the Pd (Cosman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the EEG data and citation to previous work on the Pd.

claim: Persistent current differences in the extragranular CSD were observed during the 200-250 ms interval.
source: We observe persistent current differences in the extragranular CSD during this interval sufficient to contribute to the extracortical signal.
evidence: This is supported by the CSD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No statistically significant information theoretic relationship was observed between the CSD and extracortical signal during the 200-250 ms interval.
source: However, we observed no statistically significant information theoretic relationship between the CSD and extracortical signal during this interval.
evidence: This is supported by the information theoretic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The relationship between V4 activity and the EEG does not depend on color specificity.
source: In the population average of the two calculations for each session, we observed significant information transmission during the N2pc (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). Hence, the relationship between V4 activity and the EEG does not depend on color specificity.
evidence: This is supported by the information theoretic analysis controlling for color shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Microsaccade production was not responsible for the observed information theoretic associations between signals.
source: In the population average of the two calculations for each session, we observed significant information transmission during the N2pc. Hence, microsaccade production was not responsible for the observed information theoretic associations between signals.
evidence: This is supported by the information theoretic analysis controlling for microsaccades shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The current dipole in V4 generated by the L2/3 CSD sink and the L5/6 CSD source contributes to the N2pc measured in the extracortical electric field.
source: The outcomes of these control analyses engender more confidence that the current dipole in V4 generated by the L2/3 CSD sink and the L5/6 CSD source contributes to the N2pc measured in the extracortical electric field.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the control analyses performed.

claim: V4 has a columnar organization of color tuning.
source: Given the columnar organization of color tuning of V4 neurons (Figure 5A; Roe et al., 2012; Zeki, 1973; Zeki, 1980; Tootell et al., 2004; Conway and Tsao, 2009; Kotake et al., 2009), we investigated the association between the N2pc and the CSD in columns with different color preferences.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research and Figure 5A.

claim: Gamma power reflects local circuit interactions.
source: Responses were measured as power in the gamma range (30–150 Hz) because this signal reflects local circuit interactions (Ray and Maunsell, 2011) and feature selectivity in visual cortex (Berens et al., 2008) and is more reliably measured than spiking activity across all LMA contacts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Gamma power reflects feature selectivity in visual cortex.
source: Responses were measured as power in the gamma range (30–150 Hz) because this signal reflects local circuit interactions (Ray and Maunsell, 2011) and feature selectivity in visual cortex (Berens et al., 2008) and is more reliably measured than spiking activity across all LMA contacts.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Laminar gamma power can reliably reflect feature selectivity in a spatially specific fashion.
source: This analysis collapses across differences in color tuning across layers, so although the interlaminar specificity of gamma activity is not fully understood, recent work indicates that laminar gamma power can reliably reflect feature selectivity in a spatially specific fashion (Westerberg et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: More than half of V4 columns show selectivity for red or green stimuli.
source: We found that more than half of V4 columns show selectivity for red or green stimuli (monkey Ca 12/21 [57.1%], He 5/9 [55.6%]).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on color selectivity.

claim: No difference was observed in the amplitude of the extracortical signal during the N2pc across sessions with different target and distractor colors.
source: Across sessions with different target and distractor colors, we observed no difference in the amplitude of the extracortical signal during the N2pc (paired sample t(16) = 0.40, p = 0.69) (Figure 5C) nor the laminar CSD (L2/3: t(16) = –0.85, p = 0.41; L4: t(16) = 0.75, p = 0.46; L5/6: t(16) = 0.36, p = 0.72) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the EEG and CSD data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Information transmission during the N2pc was greater when a preferred rather than a non-preferred color was in the RF.
source: However, information transmission during the N2pc was greater when a preferred rather than a non-preferred color was in the RF (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by the information theoretic analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The difference in information transmission between preferred and non-preferred colors was significant in L2/3 and L5/6 but not in L4.
source: This difference was significant in L2/3 and L5/6 but not in L4 (t test across time with at least 10 ms having p < 0.05) and is evident in single sessions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the information transmission data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant relationship was found between the difference in information transmission and columnar color selectivity index for L2/3.
source: In session-wise correlations of the difference in information transmission between preferred and non-preferred colors at the time of peak information transmission (160–180 ms) as a function of columnar color selectivity index (CCSI), we found a significant relationship for L2/3 (Spearman's R = 0.50, p = 0.005) and L5/6 (R = 0.51, p = 0.004) but not L4 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: A significant relationship was found between the difference in information transmission and columnar color selectivity index for L5/6.
source: In session-wise correlations of the difference in information transmission between preferred and non-preferred colors at the time of peak information transmission (160–180 ms) as a function of columnar color selectivity index (CCSI), we found a significant relationship for L2/3 (Spearman's R = 0.50, p = 0.005) and L5/6 (R = 0.51, p = 0.004) but not L4 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Feature selective columns transmitted significantly more information than non-feature-selective columns in all laminar compartments.
source: We found that feature selective columns, in all laminar compartments, transmitted significantly more information (Figure 5I) (two-sample t test: L2/3, p = 0.044; L4, p = 0.023; L5/6, p = 0.009).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the information transmission data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Non-selective columns were modulated with attention.
source: This was not the case, we observed that non-selective columns were modulated with attention.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on non-selective columns.

claim: Attentional modulation was observed in the CSD in L2/3 and L5/6 of non-selective columns.
source: Attentional modulation was observed in both the CSD in L2/3 and L5/6 (one-sample t test: L2/3: t(64) = –6.01, p = 9.8e–8; L4: t(64) = –0.18, p = 0.86; L5/6: t(64) = 5.24, p = 1.9e–6) as well as across all layers in the population spiking activity (one-sample t test: L2/3: t(64) = 8.00, p = 3.7e–11; L4: t(64) = 9.66, p = 4.1e–14; L5/6: t(64) = 7.58, p = 1.8e–10) during the N2pc interval (averaged 150–190 ms following array onset) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the CSD data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Attentional modulation was observed across all layers in the population spiking activity of non-selective columns.
source: Attentional modulation was observed in both the CSD in L2/3 and L5/6 (one-sample t test: L2/3: t(64) = –6.01, p = 9.8e–8; L4: t(64) = –0.18, p = 0.86; L5/6: t(64) = 5.24, p = 1.9e–6) as well as across all layers in the population spiking activity (one-sample t test: L2/3: t(64) = 8.00, p = 3.7e–11; L4: t(64) = 9.66, p = 4.1e–14; L5/6: t(64) = 7.58, p = 1.8e–10) during the N2pc interval (averaged 150–190 ms following array onset) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the spiking data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No difference was found in N2pc polarization between sessions with or without sampling of color selective columns.
source: Importantly, we tested whether the N2pc varied across sessions with or without color-selective columns sampled. We found no difference between N2pc polarization (150–190 ms after the array) between sessions with (n = 17) or without (n = 13) sampling of color selective columns (two sample t test: t(28) = –0.75, p = 0.46).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the N2pc data.

claim: Extracortical EEG spatially integrates signals from multiple cortical columns.
source: This invariance is expected because extracortical EEG spatially integrates signals from multiple cortical columns.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEG signal generation.

claim: The summed potential generated by currents along V4 columns differentiates between attention conditions simultaneous with the extracortically measured attention-associated signal.
source: The resultant potential (ERPcal) distinguished the target from a distractor in the RF throughout the N2pc (Figure 6). In other words, the summed potential generated by currents along V4 columns differentiates between attention conditions simultaneous with the extracortically measured attention-associated signal.
evidence: This is supported by the calculated ERP shown in Figure 6.

claim: The shape of the observed extracortical ERP differs from the estimated extracortical ERPcal.
source: Note that the shape of the observed extracortical ERP (ERPobs) differs from the estimated extracortical ERPcal.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 6.

claim: The ERPobs reflects several more variables such as volume-conducted contributions of nearby columns as well as the filtering and attenuating effects of the tissue and cranium above the gray matter.
source: This is expected because the ERPobs reflects several more variables such as volume-conducted contributions of nearby columns as well as the filtering and attenuating effects of the tissue and cranium above the gray matter (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEG signal generation and a citation to published research.

claim: The ERPcal does not reflect the potential contributions of other visual areas.
source: Moreover, the ERPcal does not reflect the potential contributions of other visual areas.
evidence: This is a limitation of the ERPcal calculation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The difference in ERPcal predicts the timing of the attention-associated electric field.
source: Given these expected differences, it is remarkable how well the difference in ERPcal predicts the timing of the attention-associated electric field.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of ERPcal and ERPobs shown in Figure 6.

claim: Translaminar synaptic currents in visual cortical area V4 contribute to the generation of attention-associated electric fields during visual search.
source: Using inverse modeling of cranial surface EEG and laminar resolved CSD in a cortical area, we demonstrate that translaminar synaptic currents in visual cortical area V4 contribute to the generation of attention-associated electric fields during visual search.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The dipole resulting in the attention-associated electric field stemmed from layer-specific interactions in extragranular (top-down recipient) cortical layers.
source: The dipole resulting in this electric field stemmed from layer-specific interactions in extragranular (top-down recipient) cortical layers.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The contribution of a cortical column to the overlying electric field depended on whether the visual feature in the RF matched the selectivity of the column.
source: Unexpectedly, we discovered that the contribution of a cortical column to the overlying electric field depended on whether the visual feature in the RF matched the selectivity of the column – an important consideration in the mechanism producing EEG potentials that may not be observable through the macroscopic EEG signal alone.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: It is conceivable that the N2pc arises from multiple, anatomically distinct cortical areas.
source: Given our findings regarding the functional architecture comprising attention-associated electric fields, it is conceivable that the N2pc arises from multiple, anatomically distinct cortical areas.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Electric dipoles formed across visual cortical layers could come about across multiple visual cortical areas with the relative contribution of each depending on the feature being attended to.
source: That is, given the ubiquity of columnar architecture in sensory cortex and the specificity of visual feature representations to different cortical areas, electric dipoles formed across visual cortical layers could come about across multiple visual cortical areas with the relative contribution of each depending on the feature being attended to.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study and established knowledge about cortical organization.

claim: This realization could help reconcile conflicting interpretations of the cognitive states and operations that are supposed to be indexed by the N2pc.
source: This realization could help reconcile conflicting interpretations of the cognitive states and operations that are supposed to be indexed by the N2pc (Eimer, 1996; Kiss et al., 2008; Pagano and Mazza, 2012; Foster et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study and citations to published research showing conflicting interpretations.

claim: Contributions to the N2pc from areas other than V4 are plausible because previous neurophysiological studies in macaques demonstrate attentional selection signals during visual search in the temporal, parietal, and frontal lobes.
